The Indian River County Sheriff's Office announced more than 50 arrests following a multi-agency, multi-day operation targeting human trafficking and illegal sexual activity in the county.WATCH BELOW: Indian River County Sheriff's Office reveals results of multi-agency operationOperation Late Checkout ran from Sept. 13 in Indian River County. The operation netted over 60 contacts, more than 50 arrests, and three ICE detainers, Sheriff Eric Flowers said during a press conference on Thursday.Flowers announced the results alongside a representative from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement."Agencies involved in the operation included the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, Florida Department of Law Enforcement, St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office, Seminole County Sheriff's Office, Altamonte Springs Police Department, Vero Beach Police Department, Homeland Security Investigations, Florida Office of Statewide Prosecutor and the U.S. Attorney's Office," Flowers said.The operation's targeted goal was stopping human trafficking in the Indian River County area, the sheriff's office said.During the operation, several victims were identified, and investigators said ongoing investigations are underway. Flowers said there are no specific arrests on human trafficking charges at this time.One case involved a man who traveled to Indian River County to meet a minor. Flowers said the arrest was the result of the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force working across agencies to apprehend individuals attempting to lure children online."Our team did a great job of getting him off the street," Flowers said.Undercover teams were deployed in a variety of capacities during the operation, the sheriff's office said. Victims' advocates trained to work with trafficking victims were also on hand to speak with women involved in prostitution to determine whether they were being trafficked."We have many ongoing investigations as a result of this," Flowers said.Flowers called the operation unprecedented for Indian River County."We've never had an investigation like this, to my knowledge, in Indian River County with this many agencies involved, with this many arrests in one shot," he said.FDLE Assistant Special Agent in Charge Alfonso Williams said Operation Late Checkout was initiated by FDLE in coordination with the Indian River County Sheriff's Office and is the first operation of this magnitude conducted in the county."This operation shows that within our communities there are dangerous individuals committing heinous crimes who think they can get away with it," Williams said.Williams said the operation focused on identifying human trafficking victims, reducing the demand for prostitution, and apprehending individuals seeking sexual contact with minors."Our work is far from done," Williams said. "This operation requires a lot of resources and time. We cannot do this work alone, and our success depends on the great partnership and collaboration that you see today."FDLE said it houses the Florida Trafficking Hotline. Anyone who suspects someone is a victim of trafficking can contact the hotline at 1-855-352-7233.READ OPERATION LATE CHECKOUT BELOW:

Tropical Storm Fay formed in the Atlantic Ocean Sunday morning as the system strengthened hundreds of miles southwest of the Azores.As of the 5 a.m. EDT advisory, Fay had maximum sustained winds of 45 mph and was located about 450 miles southwest of the Azores. The storm was moving north-northeast at 5 mph.Fay is a compact storm, with tropical-storm-force winds extending up to about 45 miles from its center.Forecasters at the National Hurricane Center expect Fay to strengthen further Sunday, with maximum sustained winds forecast to reach 60 mph later in the day.The storm is expected to continue moving generally north-northeast for about another day before turning toward the southwest Monday as a ridge builds to its north.Fay's opportunity to strengthen is expected to be short-lived. Increasing wind shear and dry air are forecast to cause the storm to weaken beginning Monday.The National Hurricane Center forecasts Fay to become a post-tropical remnant low by Tuesday and dissipate by the end of the week.There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect, and the storm currently poses no hazards to land.TRACKING THE TROPICS: Hurricane Center | Hurricane GuideThis story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. A West Palm Beach woman is facing multiple animal cruelty charges after investigators said 11 dogs were found living in cages containing accumulated urine and feces inside her home.Leslie Ann Torres, 34, faces seven felony counts of aggravated animal cruelty and four misdemeanor counts related to animal abandonment, according to a Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office probable cause affidavit.The investigation began Aug. 22 when deputies went to Torres' home on Glades Road while investigating an unrelated felony matter. Deputies reported smelling a strong odor of urine and feces and hearing numerous dogs barking inside.Palm Beach County Animal Care and Control was called to the home. Investigators said Torres identified 13 dogs as hers, 11 of which she ultimately surrendered to animal control.According to investigators, several dogs were being kept in wire cages containing accumulated feces, urine-soaked clothing and other debris. One cage containing approximately 4 dogs had a strong odor of urine and feces, while another cage was described as having blankets and clothing saturated with urine and feces.Investigators said some of the dogs showed signs of hair loss, skin problems and other medical issues.A veterinarian later examined all 11 surrendered dogs and reported conditions including urine staining and scalding, hair loss, skin infections, flea infestations, anemia, dehydration and malnutrition. Several dogs had body-condition scores of 2 or 3 out of 9, according to the affidavit.The veterinarian determined that all 5 recognized animal welfare freedoms had been violated and said the dogs lacked adequate room, sanitary conditions and access to clean food or water while confined in the cages, according to investigators.Investigators documented individual allegations involving several of the dogs. One dog, Chewy, was described as extremely thin with urine scalding, hair loss and a flea infestation. Another, Brownie, was described as approximately 8% dehydrated with chronic untreated skin problems.During a Sept. 9 interview, Torres told investigators she owned and cared for the dogs and maintained their confinement schedule, according to the affidavit. Investigators said she acknowledged the dogs were confined for periods of time while she worked and slept.Investigators said the buildup found inside the cages was consistent with months of accumulation rather than several days or weeks.The affidavit says the dogs' conditions improved after they were removed from Torres' care and received veterinary treatment and appropriate food, water and housing.Torres was arrested and booked into the Palm Beach County Jail.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. Ron DeSantis has set a date for the execution of the man who killed an Indian River County sheriff's deputy nearly 40 years ago. In September 1986, William Reaves shot Deputy Richard Raczkoski four times at a convenience store near Vero Beach. On Friday morning, DeSantis signed the death warrant for Reaves. I've been saying that all day. It's been a great Friday in Indian River County," Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said. Flowers never met Raczkoski. He was only 6 years old when Raczkoski was killed. But he said people still talk all the time about the man everybody knew as "Raz." "The stories that I hear are just that he was one of the best guys that we had around. He was known for having his hairbrush in his car," Flowers said. To ensure Raczkoski's legacy lives on, Flowers added a 1986 patrol car, Raz's car, to the department a few years ago. "We want people to remember that he made the ultimate sacrifice, that all of us are here today in his memory. All of us are here serving our community in the same way that he did. And it's important to never forget," Flowers said. Flowers said that's why he's been so vocal for years about wanting the death penalty for Reaves and why it meant so much when the governor's office called him Friday morning to inform him that the death warrant had been signed. It's something that's been weighing on us. You know, next week is 40 years," Flowers said. Forty years of appeals and a retrial, all resulting in the same outcome: a death sentence. The execution is scheduled for Oct. 27, a fact Flowers shared with everyone. "It was an honor to be able to make all the phone calls that came in the wake of that, to call our retirees, to call his son," Flowers said. Raczkoski's son never met his father. He was born shortly after Raczkoski was killed. Now, he knows the man responsible for murdering his father will face the death penalty. "Raz never got to see his son. And this guy has just been wasting our taxpayer dollars for the last 40 years up there. It's time to get this over with," Flowers said. Flowers said he plans to attend the execution, ensuring the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County sheriff's uniform as a reminder of what he did. A 60-year-old woman was arrested after an investigation by the Port St. Lucie Police Department in alleged exploitation and neglect of an elderly and medically vulnerable man. Barbara Baumgarten is accused of draining around $100,000 from the 85-year-old man's bank accounts and listed herself as a co-borrower on a $616,550 mortgage. She is facing felony charges of grand theft from a person 65 years of age or older, exploitation of an elderly person or disabled adult and neglect of an elderly person or disabled adult. Baumgarten was arrested with help from the U.S. On Thursday, she was booked at the St. Lucie County Jail and remains there on $310,000 bond. Her first appearance was Friday. This investigation began on March 18, when an elderly man was found injured on the floor of his Port St. Lucie home by Baumgarten, his caregiver. The victim initially reported that four men had entered his home and assaulted him. Surveillance footage showed no one entering or leaving the property, and no signs of forced entry or theft. He provided inconsistent accounts of what occurred. Detectives determined the victim was experiencing significant cognitive issues. But detectives continued looking into the victim’s overall well-being and circumstances. The investigation shifted toward concerns of elder exploitation and neglect, and grew into the months-long investigation documented in a 45-page investigative report. As the victim’s physical and cognitive health declined, he became increasingly dependent on Baumgarten, investigators found. They determined that Baumgarten had assumed significant control over the victim’s finances and legal affairs, including power of attorney and healthcare surrogate. Detectives also learned the victim had been isolated from family and friends, and that changes had been made to his estate documents that benefited Baumgarten. Records reviewed by detectives showed there was a decline in his financial accounts from $105,971 in March 2023 to approximately $4,897 by April 2026 . Investigators also uncovered a $616,550 mortgage on Baumgarten’s residence in which the victim was listed as a co-borrower. That is despite the property being solely in Baumgarten’s name and evidence that the victim was reportedly unaware his signature appeared on the mortgage. Detectives worked with healthcare providers, caregivers, family members, financial institutions and other agencies to establish the full extent of the circumstances surrounding the victim’s care and finances. The Florida Department of Children and Families ultimately substantiated allegations of exploitation and determined that the victim lacked the capacity to independently make his own decisions. The victim was removed from Baumgarten’s care, placed under a temporary guardianship, and reunited with his family. "This case serves as a reminder of the importance of looking beyond the initial circumstances when something does not appear right," the police agency said in a news release. "Through an extensive investigation, detectives were able to uncover concerns involving the care, finances, and well-being of a vulnerable member of our community and ultimately help ensure his safety. Martin County High School received another threat through the state's FortifyFL reporting system, the third bomb threat involving our campus this week, the school district said Friday afternoon. "I recognize that you have heard from me repeatedly this week regarding safety-related disruptions on our campus," Principal Lori Vogel said in a message to families. The latest threat referenced two specific buildings, requiring students and staff to be evacuated while law enforcement conducted a thorough search. Students and staff were relocated to other areas of campus during the response. On Monday, students and staff were evacuated after a bomb threat prompted a response from the Martin County Sheriff's Office. Eight days ago, students and staff were evacuated in the afternoon after a bomb threat was received via email, according to school officials. In a message sent to families, school officials said all buildings were being evacuated at the direction of law enforcement while authorities investigate the threat. Vogel noted the seriousness of the threats. "Every threat must be taken seriously," the principal said. "Each report generates a significant law enforcement response, disrupts instruction, displaces students and staff, and creates understandable concern throughout our school community. Unlike many situations that may require an emergency response, the behavior prompting these repeated disruptions is entirely avoidable. We need our families as partners in addressing this behavior. Please speak directly with your children about the seriousness and far-reaching impact of making or participating in a false threat." The message added: "What a student may view as a joke or a temporary way to avoid class can have widespread consequences for an entire campus and community. FortifyFL is an important safety resource. Students and families who become aware of a credible threat—or who have a legitimate reason to believe questionable, dangerous or criminal activity may be occurring—should continue to report that information through FortifyFL. Information about submitting a report is available on our school's and the School District's websites. "However, FortifyFL must never be used to submit information that someone knows to be false," the message said. "The District has zero tolerance for anyone who knowingly misuses the platform or participates in making a false threat. Any individual found responsible will face severe school disciplinary consequences and potential criminal charges." The principal concluded: "We appreciate your partnership in reinforcing that false threats are neither harmless nor funny. They place an unacceptable burden on students, employees, families, law enforcement and the broader community—and they must stop. Thank you for your immediate attention to this serious matter and for partnering with us to maintain a safe, orderly learning environment for every student and staff member at Martin County High School." hero.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny praised for rescue of missing woman in Gadsden County
hero.body:
An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his bloodhound partner who helped find a missing 84-year-old woman with dementia in Gadsden County last month have returned home to praise from their agency for responding to the mutual-aid call while away for training. Deputy Sam Lewis and K9 Penny joined bloodhound search teams from across the state in Gadsden County near Tallahassee, where they were attending a K9 certification course when Margaret Myles Ellis was reported missing on Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before.

Officials said Ellis had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Multiple dogs participated in the rotated search effort, with Penny and other bloodhounds taking turns searching for the missing woman. Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area to assist in the search. Ellis was found approximately 30 hours later in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety.

Lt. Eric Jaworski of the Indian River County Sheriff's Office praised Deputy Lewis for responding to the emergency despite being nine counties away. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Jaworski said. He emphasized that Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny were fortunate to be in the right place at the right time. "Luckily, they were at the right place at the right time. We're extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and our entire K9 unit that, you know, goes out every day," Jaworski said.

The Indian River County Sheriff's Office K9 unit includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. Jaworski also highlighted the unique role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies within the agency. "Dogs don't judge you, you know they love everybody, so it's a good way to connect and it opens up the door to express some of these things that we see and hear every day," he said. Ellis was reunited with her family following the rescue, and Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned to Indian River County and resumed their regular duties.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council advances $2.2 billion 2050 Mobility Plan on first reading
hero.teaser: Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that includes an updated mobility fee schedule and a 25-year vision for roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit.
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint that includes an updated mobility fee schedule and a 25-year vision for roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. The plan requires final approval from the City Council before taking effect on Dec. 31.

The plan serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050 to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid population growth. The city acknowledged the plan remains $1.7 billion short of full funding.

Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the challenge growth presents to city finances. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said.

The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees, which are applied to new development and paid by developers. The updated plan includes a mobility fee schedule for the next four years. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

A city official addressed the funding gap during the council meeting. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said.

The city said more than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020. The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid-, and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes.

Resident Laura Milsom said the growth is impossible to ignore on local roads. "The population increased so rapidly," Milsom said. "A lot of traffic backups." Milsom said she supports the fee approach. "Anyone wanting to come in and develop in the area should be partly responsible for how the traffic is managed and everything," Milsom said.

cards.headline: Fort Pierce police confirm three Avenue L shootings striking homes are linked and targeted
cards.body:
Fort Pierce police say three recent shootings that struck multiple homes along Avenue L are connected and targeted, and investigators have already identified suspects. The shootings happened Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18. While no one was hurt, several homes were hit by gunfire, including one where a mother and her four children were inside.

Fort Pierce police say evidence shows all three shootings are related. Major Mike Santiago said the means and methods used, the shooting, and the types of weapons used are all similar in all of these cases. He said it is a matter of drilling down on some of these details to develop enough probable cause. Santiago said the particular homes and the people involved have histories, which is how investigators are starting to develop the case.

A Fort Pierce home where a mother and her four children were inside was hit by gunfire, including bullets that entered her teenage son's bedroom Friday night. Officers with the Fort Pierce Police Department responded to the home around 9:07 p.m. They found multiple bullet holes outside the home, with several rounds making their way inside through walls and windows. The mother, who asked not to be identified, said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. She said she has little kids and they are terrified. She said any noise keeps her from sleeping.

According to police, the family's home was struck three times within days, first on Tuesday and then twice more on Friday. A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she narrowly escaped being struck during one of the shootings. Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home. The teen, who asked not to be identified out of fear of retaliation, said she was outside when the gunfire erupted. She said she tried to run in the house, and with it raining that day she ended up falling on the floor. She said when she fell on the floor that is when the bullet went in the house, and if she had not fallen, she would have been hit.

The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for bomb threat, fourth in 10 days
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, the fourth threat against the school in just over a week. The student, identified as Noah Taylor, told investigators he was just tired of being in class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office.

Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip claimed someone was walking by the boys bathroom and overheard talk of bombs in the school that would blow up in third period. The tipster also reported hearing about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to Taylor, who initially denied involvement and suggested someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed and explained he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to Budensiek.

Taylor was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services in Fort Pierce. The arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against Martin County High School. The initial threat came through Russia, Budensiek said, and the last two remain under investigation with more arrests potentially forthcoming.

Budensiek issued a warning to students considering similar threats. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

The arrest comes six weeks into the academic year as authorities signal that all threats, even those intended as pranks, will be met with severe consequences.

cards.headline: More than 1,000 volunteers turn out for Martin County beach cleanup
cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.

Keep Martin Beautiful is the local coordinator of the International Coastal Cleanup. The nonprofit volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful.

County volunteers participated at 28 locations, including Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris. Linda Emerson said at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island that by picking up pieces of plastic, volunteers can realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie advances $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B funding gap
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved first reading Monday of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan, a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint designed to address traffic congestion and accommodate population growth through 2050. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years, but city officials acknowledged a $1.7 billion funding gap remains. Final approval is required before the plan takes effect Dec. 31.

The plan outlines projects including new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, according to the city. Mayor Shannon Martin said growth has strained city finances. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said.

Mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers fund the infrastructure projects. Resident Laura Milsom said the rapid expansion has brought traffic backups. "The population increased so rapidly," Milsom said. "A lot of traffic backups." She said she supports making developers partly responsible for traffic management.

A city official told council members during Monday's meeting that the plan cannot solve all funding problems. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said.

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid- and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. "Mobility fees may need to supplement that," Samples said.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for bomb threat to skip class, fourth in under two weeks
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday and charged with a second-degree felony after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app because he wanted to get out of class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The incident marks the fourth threat against the school in just a week and a half, and Sheriff Jon Budensiek said more arrests may follow.

The school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip read, "I was walking by the boys bathroom, and they were saying there is bombs in the school and that they are going to blow up in third period today." The tipster also claimed to hear about a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks.

Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus. When first confronted, the student denied involvement and said maybe somebody else sent the tip. After further questioning, the student confessed, telling investigators he just wanted to get out of third-period class, Budensiek said.

The arrest is not connected to the three other recent threats against the school. Budensiek said the initial threat came through Russia, and investigators are still working on the last two cases. "We could potentially be making some more arrests on that case," he said.

The student was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services in Fort Pierce. Budensiek issued a stern warning to students who might consider making similar threats. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

The arrest comes six weeks into the academic year as the school district confronts a wave of threats.

cards.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny rescue missing woman in Gadsden County
cards.teaser: Deputy Sam Lewis and bloodhound Penny helped locate an 84-year-old woman with dementia in shallow water after 30 hours missing while attending K9 training near Tallahassee.
cards.body:
An Indian River County sheriff's deputy and his bloodhound partner helped rescue an 84-year-old woman with dementia in Gadsden County after the woman had been missing for 30 hours. Deputy Sam Lewis and K9 Penny were attending a K9 certification course near Tallahassee when they joined the search effort for Margaret Myles Ellis.

Ellis was reported missing Sept. 15 after last being seen at her home the day before. She had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Bloodhound search teams from across the state participated in the search, rotating dogs through the effort.

Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured the moment he scaled down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area. Ellis was found in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety. "They're coming out," the body camera footage captured.

Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised the deputy's response. "They're nine counties away, and that's why we're proud of him and all of our deputies because no matter where they are, in the state or in the nation, they are always willing to help," Sheriff Eric Flowers said. He expressed pride in the entire K9 unit, which includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy. Ellis was reunited with her family. Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned home and resumed their duties.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council advances $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B funding gap
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council approved the first reading of the city's 2050 Mobility Plan on Monday, advancing a $2.2 billion infrastructure blueprint to address traffic congestion and accommodate rapid growth through 2050. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years but still faces a $1.7 billion funding shortfall. Final approval is required before the plan takes effect Dec. 31.

The 25-year plan outlines new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit projects. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, and Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge that growth presents. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said. Mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners, fund the infrastructure projects. Scott Samples with the city said increasing mobility fees is one tool to help fund future projects. A city official told the council the plan cannot solve all funding problems but identifies needs through 2050 based on current analysis.

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-term, mid-term and long-term projects. Short-term projects through 2030 include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. Samples said mobility fees may need to supplement that project. The official explained that while the city knows there is not enough money to fund every single project in the mobility plan, the plan is intended to identify needs through 2050 based on current analysis and serves as one piece of the funding puzzle.

Resident Laura Milsom said the population increased rapidly and has caused traffic backups. She said the community is not in love with the traffic situation and noted the rapid expansion has come with consequences. Milsom said anyone wanting to develop in the area should be partly responsible for how traffic is managed. The plan serves as a road map for building infrastructure projects through 2050 as the city works to accommodate continued growth while managing significant funding constraints.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

Rehki Jyquan Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge following the stop near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21.

A deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier. Deputies saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

hero.headline: Fort Pierce police link three Avenue L shootings, identify suspects
hero.body:
Fort Pierce police have confirmed that three shootings along Avenue L are connected and targeted, with investigators already identifying suspects as they work to develop probable cause for arrests. The shootings occurred on Tuesday, September 15 and twice more on Friday, September 18, striking several homes including one where a mother and her four children lived.

Major Mike Santiago said evidence shows all three shootings are related. "The means and the methods that were used, the shooting, the types of weapons that were used are all similar in in all of these cases," Santiago said. "It's a matter of drilling down on some of these details so that we can develop enough probable cause. But I can tell you that these particular homes and the people that are involved do have histories and that's how we're starting to develop the case as it as it starts to unfold."

The mother whose home was struck three times within days said bullets entered her teenage son's bedroom during the Friday night shooting around 9:07 p.m. "It was pretty close because if he would have jumped he would've got hit," she said. Officers found at least 10 bullet holes in the front of the home, with several rounds penetrating walls and windows. The woman said she and her children immediately dropped to the ground as bullets flew through their home. "I have little kids and they are terrified," she said. "Any noise...I can't even sleep." She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said.

A neighboring home and another house across the street were also hit by gunfire. A 17-year-old girl who lives next door said she was outside when the gunfire erupted and narrowly escaped being struck. "All I know is I turned around and I turned around again and they just went shooting and I tried to run in the house. With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." Bullet holes shattered the windows on the side of her home.

Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. No one was hurt in any of the shootings.

With it raining that day I ended up falling on the floor and when I fell on the floor that's when the bullet went in the house," the girl said. "If I didn't fall, I would've got hit." The mother whose home was repeatedly targeted said arrests cannot come soon enough. She now plans to move her family out of the neighborhood as quickly as possible. "I'm just trying to get out of here. That's all I can do," she said. Young kids getting hold of weapons, guns, stuff like that, it's just beyond me." Police have increased patrols in the area and are asking anyone with information about the shootings or those involved to contact the Fort Pierce Police Department. Police have not released information about the suspects or possible motive. The investigation is ongoing.

hero.headline: Martin County High sophomore Noah Taylor charged with felony for false bomb threat
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School sophomore was arrested Tuesday after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat through the school safety app because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

According to the Martin County Sheriff's Office, the threat was submitted through FortifyFL around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present at the school. The message read, "I was walking by the boys bathroom and they were saying there was bombs in the school and that they were going to blow up in third period today," Sheriff John Budensiek said during a news conference.

The school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and began investigating. Surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. Another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. When questioned, Taylor initially blamed other students but could not provide identifying information about them and eventually admitted making the report. "He gave the explanation of this threat as to why he gave the threat as he just wanted to get out of third period class. He was just tired of being in class," Budensiek said. Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before transporting him to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce.

The arrest marks the fourth threat connected to Martin County High School in just over a week and a half, but investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. "At this point, we cannot connect him to the other three bomb threats that we have. The initial threat came in, we know it came in through Russia, and then the last two we're still investigating," the sheriff said. Principal Lori Vogel emphasized the impact of false threats in a statement. "False threats are neither harmless nor funny. False threats can cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement," Vogel said. Budensiek warned students that what may seem like a joke can carry long-term consequences, including possible expulsion and difficulty finding employment. The sheriff's office said anonymous threats made through text messages, online platforms and other electronic communications can still be traced and investigated.

cards.headline: Palm City SWAT standoff: Arrest report details Darrel Abbey's gun threats, prison comment
cards.teaser: New arrest report details from the Martin County Sheriff's Office reveal that Darrel Abbey pointed a gun at his ex-girlfriend multiple times, threatened to kill her and her stepfather, and stated he would not return to prison before the hours-long standoff.
cards.body:
An arrest report from the Martin County Sheriff's Office released following an hours-long SWAT standoff in Palm City reveals that Darrel Abbey pointed a gun at his ex-girlfriend multiple times, threatened to kill her and her stepfather, and said he was not going back to prison.

The ex-girlfriend arrived at Abbey's home at about 12:08 p.m. after the two had broken up the previous night. She told investigators Abbey was not doing well mentally and had previously made comments about killing himself. When she arrived, Abbey had a rifle in his Tesla and a 10 mm handgun in his shorts. Abbey appeared to be extremely intoxicated, according to the report.

Abbey brought both firearms inside the home and began screaming at the woman while holding a gun. He pointed the gun at her several times and threatened to kill her and her stepfather. At one point, Abbey placed the gun under his chin and pulled the trigger, but the firearm did not discharge because the magazine had been removed. Abbey later began packing his vehicle. Fearing he was going to shoot her stepfather, the woman took the gun away from him, but Abbey continued reaching for it as she begged him to stop. When Abbey picked up the gun again, he said it was really dangerous now.

Abbey continued drinking bourbon and Jameson throughout the encounter. He walked outside and the woman heard several loud pop sounds. Abbey returned inside to retrieve a rifle and tried to get the woman to come outside and shoot it with him. When she asked what he was shooting at, Abbey told her he had hung a bucket from a nearby tree and was shooting at it.

At some point, Abbey began cleaning the firearms and said he had to wipe all his fingerprints off and get the gunshot residue off of his hands because he was not going back to prison. Abbey later attempted to get into his vehicle while continuing to drink. The woman began recording him. Abbey appeared intoxicated while sitting in the driver's seat, slurred his words and struggled to hold his head upright. When Abbey realized the woman was recording, he reached for her phone. The woman then ran down the road until a passing motorist stopped to help her.

Deputies later attempted to contact Abbey at the residence, but he refused to open the door or speak with them, leading to an hours-long standoff involving the Martin County Sheriff's Office SWAT team and hostage negotiators. Abbey was booked into the Martin County Jail without bond on charges including battery and aggravated assault with a deadly weapon without intent to kill. Abbey is a convicted felon from Washington state with a prior conviction for vehicular assault.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for bomb threat to skip class, sheriff says
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday on a felony charge after confessing to sending a fake bomb threat through the Fortify Florida app, telling investigators he just wanted to get out of third-period class, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office. The arrest marks the fourth threat against the school in 10 days.

Sheriff Jon Budensiek said the school resource officer received the threat around 9 a.m. Tuesday. The tip claimed someone overheard talk of bombs in the school set to explode during third period, including a bomb in a trash can and fireworks in backpacks. Investigators reviewed security camera footage and traced the electronic submission back to the student on campus.

The student initially denied involvement and suggested someone else may have sent the tip. After further questioning, he confessed that he just wanted to get out of third-period class, Budensiek said. The student was transported to the Department of Juvenile Services facility in Fort Pierce.

Budensiek confirmed the arrest is not connected to three other recent threats against Martin County High School. The first threat came through Russia, he said, and investigators are still working the last two cases with potential additional arrests. The school district is six weeks into the academic year.

Budensiek issued a warning to students considering similar threats. "This really is catastrophic for your life," he said. "This individual's been arrested for a felony. He's been transported to DYS in Fort Pierce. He's going to have strong repercussions from the school, if not expulsion, and it will affect his ability to get jobs down the road. While it may come across as a joke, we have to take these serious."

cards.headline: Indian River County deputy, K9 Penny help rescue missing Gadsden County woman
cards.teaser: Deputy Sam Lewis and his bloodhound partner Penny joined a multi-county search that located an 84-year-old woman with dementia in shallow water after 30 hours missing.
cards.body:
Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Sam Lewis and his K9 partner Penny helped rescue an 84-year-old woman with dementia during a search in Gadsden County near Tallahassee. The deputy and his bloodhound were attending a K9 certification course when they joined the effort to locate Margaret Myles Ellis, who had been missing for approximately 30 hours.

Ellis was last seen at her home on Sept. 14 and reported missing on Sept. 15. She had been diagnosed with early-stage dementia and has a pacemaker. Body camera footage from Deputy Lewis captured him scaling down trees into a ditch in a heavily wooded area during the search. Ellis was found in shallow water, and Deputy Lewis helped pull her to safety.

Bloodhound search teams from across the state participated in the effort. Penny searched along with other dogs in a rotated dog search, according to officials. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers praised Lewis and the department's K9 unit for their willingness to help no matter where they are. The sheriff's office K9 unit includes 18 dogs trained for patrol, search and rescue, explosives detection, electronics detection, firearms detection and therapy.

Ellis was reunited with her family after the rescue. Deputy Lewis and K9 Penny have since returned to Indian River County and resumed their duties. Sheriff's officials highlighted the role of therapy dogs in supporting deputies, noting that dogs provide a way for law enforcement to connect and express the experiences they encounter daily. The sheriff said the department is extremely proud of Deputy Lewis and the entire K9 unit that goes out every day.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie council approves $2.2 billion mobility plan on first reading
hero.body:
Port St. Lucie City Council on Monday approved the first reading of a $2.2 billion mobility plan designed to address traffic congestion and accommodate population growth through 2050, though the city faces a $1.7 billion funding gap. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years and outlines a 25-year vision for infrastructure development. The updated plan requires final council approval before taking effect on Dec. 31.

The 2050 Mobility Plan serves as a road map for infrastructure projects including new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit. More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, creating visible traffic problems on local roads. Resident Laura Milsom said the population increased rapidly and caused traffic backups. Short-term projects looking ahead to 2030 include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes.

Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge facing the city. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said. The infrastructure projects are funded by mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners. Milsom said she supports that approach, stating that anyone wanting to develop in the area should be partly responsible for how traffic is managed. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

Despite the mobility fee structure, the city says the plan is still $1.7 billion short of full funding. A city official addressed the gap during the council meeting, explaining that the plan cannot solve all problems from a funding perspective but represents one piece of the puzzle. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said. The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-term, mid-term and long-term projects to accommodate continued growth in the city.

hero.headline: Execution date set for Oct. 27 for killer of Indian River County deputy
hero.body:
Governor Ron DeSantis signed a death warrant Friday for William Reaves, who was convicted of killing Indian River County Sheriff's Deputy Richard Raczkoski in 1986. Reaves is scheduled to be executed Oct. 27. Indian River County Sheriff Eric Flowers said he plans to attend the execution and wants to make sure the last thing Reaves sees is an Indian River County deputy uniform. The execution would mark Florida's 18th this year, following 19 executions in 2025.

Marc Raczkoski, the victim's brother, said the signed warrant brings closure after 40 years of waiting. Marc Raczkoski was 22 years old when his 29-year-old brother was killed. He said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family, with his parents ending traditions like Christmas trees and holiday decorations. "It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." Marc recalled the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything, when a friend from the police department drove him to the hospital but kept him in the car too long, which made him realize his brother had not survived.

Deputy Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County on Feb. 23, 1986. He was shot four times and killed. Authorities arrested Reaves days later in Albany, Georgia. Reaves, who was 37 at the time, was extradited to Indian River County and confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he panicked when a gun fell out of his shorts and that he was under the influence of drugs. Reaves was convicted of murder in 1987 and sentenced to death. Marc said his brother was calling a cab for Reaves when he was killed. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me," Marc said.

Flowers said the coming execution will bring healing to the agency. Marc Raczkoski described his brother as someone always focused on public service who was quick to make people laugh and enjoyed fishing and the outdoors. Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said her group has concerns about the pace of executions and the transparency of the selection process. "We don't know how people are being chosen for execution or why," Hanna said. Deputy Raczkoski is buried at Hillcrest Memorial Gardens in Fort Pierce.

"Richard Raczkoski, beloved son, corporal, sheriff's department, Indian River County," reads Marc Raczkoski, blinking back tears. "I was 22," Marc said quietly. "I was 22." It's always been an agonizing place for Marc — one that's brought up too many painful memories. Yet this time, his grief feels a little lighter. This time, for the first time in the 40 years he's come to visit his older brother, he finally has the answer he's been longing to give. And it's finally over," Marc said.Gov. Ron DeSantis on Friday signed the death warrant for William Reaves, the man convicted of killing Raczkoski in 1986. If carried out, the execution will mark Florida's 18th this year. 20, and Reaves has one last chance at an appeal."It gives closure," Marc said. "Now, when everybody asks me, 'What happened to the guy that murdered my brother?' That the first question I get, and I got to say, 'He's still — still hasn't happened." "You'll finally have a different answer," investigative reporter Kate Hussey supplied. "Yes, finally have a different answer," Marc replied. 23, 1986, 29-year-old Deputy Richard Raczkoski answered a 911 call at a convenience store in Indian River County. Minutes later, he was shot four times and killed, launching a multi-agency manhunt for the killer.Days later, authorities arrested 37-year-old William Reaves in Albany, Georgia, who was extradited to Indian River County, where he confessed to killing Raczkoski, saying he "panicked" when a gun fell out of his shorts, and that he was under the influence of drugs at the time. Forty years later, Marc said the memories of that night are still fresh and painful, recalling the middle-of-the-night knock on the door that changed everything. "One of the friends that was on the police department in Fort Pierce, my brother's friend, was at the back door. He took me up in the car and raced me up to the hospital, but I knew when they were talking to me in there for too long, I knew he didn't make it. I knew he didn't make it, and from then, it was just a blur of everything else after that," Marc told WPTV. "How could somebody do something like that? Richard was calling him a cab, for God's sake's. To empty his gun into him is beyond me. How could somebody do something like that?" Feels like everybody forgot," Marc said.Marc said the years without resolution took a toll on his entire family."It's something I wouldn't wish on anybody to have to go through. And watch your parents go through," Marc said. "No more Christmas trees in the house. Holidays were never the same. Mom didn't decorate." It's finally over," Marc said.The news also brought relief to the Indian River County Sheriff's Office, and Sheriff Eric Flowers himself, who has pushed for Reaves' death warrant to be signed. I think it's going to be a moment of healing for our agency," Flowers told WPTV. Flowers said he plans to attend Reaves' execution. We also don't know the impact this is having on corrections staff and those who are involved," Grace Hanna of Floridians Against the Death Penalty said.Hanna, though, knows the pain Raczkowski's family is experiencing. "Though certainly don't hold any ill will towards those who feel that this is what gives them closure." "Mom and Dad didn't see any closure in this, time that they didn't get to spend with him, time he didn't get to spend with my children, his nieces and nephews. It's all very much to take in." Marc described his brother as someone always focused on public service. "He was quick to make you laugh. He was always focused on public service, to serve people. He had found a man — an elderly man — that wandered away from a facility one time, and he's the one that found him out in the woods by the facility," Marc recalled. "He liked to fish and he liked the outdoors. And he was just basically fun to be around." Yet as he walks away from the grave, knowing the grief will never go away, he hopes the coming execution will bring something he has long sought."There is finally closure for Richard," Marc said. cards.headline: Vero Beach man faces felony charge for illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
cards.teaser: A 20-year-old Vero Beach man was arrested early Monday after a traffic stop near Americana and 90th Avenue led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
cards.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested 20-year-old Rehki Jyquan Hughes early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana. Hughes faces a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge.

According to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit, a deputy stopped a black Dodge sedan near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 after noticing the vehicle had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows. The deputy said he smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window. Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier.

Deputies said they saw what appeared to be marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

hero.headline: Port St. Lucie Council approves first reading of $2.2B mobility plan with $1.7B funding gap
hero.teaser: The Port St. Lucie City Council gave first-reading approval Monday to a $2.2 billion 2050 Mobility Plan aimed at addressing traffic congestion and growth, though the city acknowledges a $1.7 billion funding shortfall.
hero.body:
The Port St. Lucie City Council gave first-reading approval Monday to a $2.2 billion 2050 Mobility Plan aimed at addressing traffic congestion and growth, though the city acknowledges a $1.7 billion funding shortfall. The plan updates the mobility fee schedule for the next four years and outlines a broader 25-year vision that includes new and improved roads, sidewalks, trails, bike lanes and transit through 2050.

More than 65,000 people have moved to Port St. Lucie since 2020, according to the city. Mayor Shannon Martin acknowledged the financial challenge growth presents. "We know that growth has never paid for itself," Martin said.

The infrastructure projects in the plan are funded by mobility fees applied to new development and paid by developers, not homeowners. Resident Laura Milsom said she supports that approach. "Anyone wanting to come in and develop in the area should be partly responsible for how the traffic is managed and everything," Milsom said. Milsom said the rapid expansion has created traffic backups on local roads.

A city official addressed the funding gap during the council meeting. "We fully know that there's not enough money to fund every single project that's in the mobility plan. But the mobility plan is intended to say, through 2050, here's the needs that we see based on our analysis today. And so it's, it can't solve all of the problems funding-wise, but it's a piece of the puzzle," the official said. Scott Samples with the City of Port St. Lucie said increasing mobility fees is one way to help fund future projects. "They're one of the tools in our toolbox," Samples said. "Help create the funding necessary to build the infrastructure that we need to, you know, maintain, but also to grow."

The plan breaks infrastructure improvements into short-, mid-, and long-term projects. Short-term projects look ahead to 2030 and include expanding St. Lucie West Boulevard from four to six lanes. The updated plan requires final approval from the City Council before taking effect on Dec. 31.

cards.headline: Port St. Lucie MRI tech told sedated patient 'nobody can see what I do to you,' criminal complaint says
cards.body:
A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital allegedly told the woman "Nobody can see what I can do to you" before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a Port St. Lucie police criminal complaint.

Gabriel Cruz, 42, faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. The patient told investigators she woke up during the assault and alleged Cruz was rubbing her hair afterward, then cleaned her mouth with a white towel, the complaint states.

Port St. Lucie police responded to HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital shortly after 8 a.m. on Sept. 14 after the patient reported the assault. The patient had been admitted after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. She told police medication made her drowsy and that she drifted in and out of sleep when she was transported for an MRI at about 4 p.m. The patient, whose primary language is Spanish, described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt.

"In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," Port St. Lucie Police Chief Leo Niemczyk said.

Hospital staff identified Cruz as a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there, but the video showed Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time.

"Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Niemczyk said.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital released a statement saying the facility contacted law enforcement and ended Cruz's assignment when the allegation was reported. The hospital said it has assisted law enforcement throughout the investigation and remains focused on supporting the patient.

"It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital," Niemczyk said.

Julie Stoyka, director of the Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee, said the impact of such assaults can bring feelings of shame, fear, confusion, guilt and anger. The program's rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

cards.headline: Card skimmer discovered on 7-Eleven gas pump in Fort Pierce prompts investigation
cards.teaser: A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation.
cards.body:
A cybersecurity professional found a card skimming device on a gas pump at a 7-Eleven on Orange Avenue in Fort Pierce on Monday morning, prompting a police investigation. Arlo Bess said he routinely checks for card skimmers before using gas pumps and discovered the device after pulling on the card reader.

"So, I pulled the card reader out and it took a little bit of pull, a couple pounds of pull because it was just stuck in there. It wasn't much at all, and when I got it, I was at first very surprised," Bess said. "I'm just naturally paranoid, if you would, from all my work and training." After finding the device, he locked his truck and informed the store manager. "She was equally surprised and said she had never seen one before," he added.

Fort Pierce Police Major Michael Santiago said the department is investigating the incident. "We try to track it back to whoever may own that particular skimmer. We also check our systems to see if there's something going on in the neighboring jurisdictions, if they've had similar incidents," Santiago said. "We conducted intense screening of video surveillance from the actual location to try and identify who may have installed this particular device. I can tell you it's a little difficult because we simply don't know when it was installed."

Card skimmers are devices that criminals attach to legitimate card readers to steal card information, including PINs. "On the inside of that skimmer, it's got a little microchip in there, and typically they'll have like a Bluetooth connectivity piece in there. When you slide your card in there, it actually reads the mag stripe off the card and it will intercept that information," Bess said. He noted that no other gas pumps at the station had card skimmers.

Santiago and Bess warned that card skimmers can also be found on ATM machines, where criminals may use pinhole cameras to capture PINs. "Typically, if it's an ATM machine, you've got a debit card, and you have a PIN that you have to put in. So, they'll also have these little pin cameras that will take a picture and watch you actually putting your PIN into the ATM machine," Bess said.

hero.headline: Martin County High student arrested for false bomb threat, fourth targeting school in week
hero.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday on a felony charge after investigators say he submitted a false bomb threat through the FortifyFL school safety reporting system because he wanted to get out of class. Noah Taylor, a sophomore, faces a charge of making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony.

The threat was submitted around 9:29 a.m. Tuesday while a resource deputy was present at the school. The message stated someone was walking by the boys bathroom and heard people saying there were bombs in the school that would blow up during third period. Sheriff John Budensiek said the school resource deputy quickly determined the threat originated from inside the school and immediately began investigating.

Surveillance footage and witness interviews led investigators to Taylor. Another student told deputies Taylor had said the tip would be submitted anonymously and would not be traced back to him. Investigators said Taylor was questioned and initially blamed other students, but he could not provide identifying information about those students and eventually admitted making the report. Taylor told deputies he made the threat because he was tired of being in class and wanted to get out of third period. Deputies confiscated Taylor's laptop as evidence before taking him into custody. He was later transported to the Department of Juvenile Justice Juvenile Assessment Center in Fort Pierce.

The arrest marks the fourth bomb threat connected to Martin County High School in just over a week and a half. Budensiek said investigators have not linked Taylor to the other three cases. The initial threat came through Russia, and the last two remain under investigation. Principal Lori Vogel said in a statement that false threats cause fear, disrupt learning and place a burden on students, families, school employees and law enforcement. Budensiek warned that what students think is funny can have long-term consequences, including difficulty getting a job in the future. School officials said the threat was quickly determined to be a hoax and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation.

cards.headline: More than 1,000 volunteers turn out for Martin County beach cleanup
cards.teaser: More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup.
cards.body:
More than 1,000 volunteers participated in a beach cleanup throughout Martin County on Saturday as part of the International Coastal Cleanup. Keep Martin Beautiful coordinated the local effort across 28 locations.

The nonprofit, volunteer-based community action organization was founded in 1994 as an affiliate of Keep America Beautiful. County volunteers participated at Stuart Beach, Hobe Sound Beach, Jensen Beach, Jensen Causeway, Bob Graham Beach, Sandsprit Park, and Indian Riverside Park.

Keep Martin Beautiful said the cleanup helps protect birds and marine life by reducing the likelihood that these creatures will become injured or entangled in plastics or ingest deadly debris.

Linda Emerson participated at Blowing Rocks Preserve on Jupiter Island. She said picking up pieces of plastic allows people to realize how much they are using in their own lives and choose to make a difference.

hero.headline: Vero Beach man arrested with loaded pistol, illegal Glock switch after traffic stop
hero.teaser: Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.
hero.body:
Indian River County deputies arrested a 20-year-old Vero Beach man early Monday after a traffic stop led to the discovery of a machine gun conversion device, a loaded pistol and marijuana.

Rehki Jyquan Hughes was stopped near Americana and 90th Avenue shortly after midnight Sept. 21 when a deputy noticed his black Dodge sedan had no visible tag lights and heavily tinted windows, according to an Indian River County Sheriff's Office arrest affidavit. The deputy smelled fresh and burnt marijuana after Hughes lowered his window.

Hughes told the deputy he had smoked marijuana a few hours earlier. Deputies said they saw marijuana packaging and a marijuana stem inside the vehicle. Hughes showed deputies a photo of an expired medical marijuana card. Dispatch confirmed Hughes was on the medical marijuana registry but did not have an active order allowing him to possess marijuana, deputies said.

As Hughes got out of the car, deputies said he repeatedly reached toward his pocket despite being told not to. A metal device fell from his pocket. An ATF task force officer who responded to the scene identified the device as a machine gun conversion device, commonly called a Glock switch, deputies said. The report says the device can alter a firearm to allow automatic fire. Under Florida law, an unattached device of that kind is classified as a bump stock.

A search of the vehicle turned up a loaded FN 5.7 pistol with one round in the chamber and 19 rounds in the magazine, deputies said. The gun was found in a bag Hughes had been reaching toward, according to the affidavit. Deputies also reported finding multiple bags of marijuana, a marijuana nugget and two marijuana cigarette ends.

Hughes denied knowing about the gun or conversion device but admitted the marijuana was his, the report said. Hughes was arrested on a felony charge of possessing a bump stock and a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge. The firearm, ammunition, device and suspected marijuana were submitted into evidence, according to the sheriff's office.

cards.headline: MRI tech told sedated patient 'nobody can see what I do to you' at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital
cards.body:
A traveling MRI technician accused of sexually assaulting a sedated patient at HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital told the woman "Nobody can see what I can do to you" before bringing her into an MRI room, according to a criminal complaint filed by Port St. Lucie police.

Gabriel Cruz, 42, faces a first-degree felony charge of sexual battery involving a physically helpless or incapacitated victim. The complaint details what police say happened Sept. 14 when officers responded to the hospital shortly after 8 a.m. after a patient reported being sexually assaulted by a technician.

The patient told investigators she had been admitted to the hospital after experiencing fainting spells and two falls that caused her to hit her head. She was transported from her room for an MRI at about 4 p.m. Medication made her drowsy and she drifted in and out of sleep, according to the report. She described the technician as a Hispanic man with a medium build who spoke Spanish and wore a blue shirt. The patient told police that after the MRI, she fell asleep. When she woke up, she alleged the technician had sexually assaulted her and was rubbing her hair. The report states he then cleaned her mouth with a white towel.

"In this case our victim was pretty aware of what was going on. She was just not physically able to do much about it. She woke up while the act was occurring," said Leo Niemczyk, Port St. Lucie police chief. "It was just particularly troubling because it was a vulnerable person who was under sedation and it was in a hospital setting and we all want to feel safe when we're in a hospital."

Hospital staff identified the technician as Gabriel Cruz, a traveling technician who had been under contract at the hospital since August. Police said surveillance video does not show inside the MRI room because there are no cameras there. However, the video showed that Cruz was the only person in the room with the patient during that time, according to the report.

"Often times when you see this type of behavior it may not have been their first time, right? So we always have to be aware that there may be other victims out there," Chief Niemczyk said.

Julie Stoyka, director of the Sexual Assault Assistance Program of the Treasure Coast and Okeechobee, said victims can feel ashamed, fearful, confused, guilty and angry. The program's rape crisis helpline is staffed 24 hours a day, seven days a week.

HCA Florida St. Lucie Hospital released a statement saying the facility does not tolerate behavior that jeopardizes patient safety or security. When the allegation was reported, the hospital contacted law enforcement and ended Cruz's assignment. The hospital said it has assisted law enforcement throughout the investigation and remains focused on supporting the patient.

cards.headline: 15-year-old arrested after false bomb threat at Martin County High School
cards.teaser: A 15-year-old Martin County High School student confessed to sending a hoax bomb threat that disrupted the school Tuesday, authorities said. The arrest comes amid multiple recent school threats in the area.
cards.body:
A 15-year-old Martin County High School student was arrested Tuesday after confessing to sending a false bomb threat to the school, according to the Martin County Sheriff's Office and school district.

Noah Taylor, a sophomore at the school, was charged with making a false report concerning the planting of a bomb, a second-degree felony. School resource officers and Criminal Investigations Division detectives traced the message back to Taylor, who confessed to sending the threat during the investigation, according to the Sheriff's Office.

The threat was reported through FortifyFL, Principal Lori Vogel told families. The threat was quickly determined to be a hoax, and students and staff remained safe throughout the investigation, according to the school district. The Sheriff's Office immediately began investigating and identified the apparent source of the message. The district notified families Tuesday that an arrest had been made after initially telling parents an arrest appeared imminent.

The arrest comes after multiple hoax bomb threats involving schools in the area in recent weeks, according to the Sheriff's Office. Investigators said they can only link Taylor to this specific threat.

School officials said students found to have been involved in making threats could face both school disciplinary action and legal consequences. The district reminded families that FortifyFL is an important tool for reporting legitimate safety concerns, but knowingly submitting false information or making a false threat can have serious consequences.

False threats are neither harmless nor funny, Vogel said. She added that they can cause fear, disrupt learning, and place a burden on students, families, school employees, and law enforcement. The Sheriff's Office said threats made anonymously, through text messages, online, or through other electronic communications, can still be traced and investigated.
